title: What are common caching mistakes — caching everything, assuming `cache()` is eager, caching data used once, forgetting `unpersist()`, confusing `cache()` with `collect()`, thinking cache eliminates shuffle?

s1_definition.profdef: Common Spark caching mistakes include caching everything indiscriminately, which causes memory pressure and eviction; assuming cache is eager when it is lazy and does nothing until an action; caching data that is used only once, which wastes memory for no reuse benefit; forgetting to unpersist in long-running applications, which lets caches accumulate until storage is exhausted; confusing cache, which stores partitions distributed on executors, with collect, which pulls all data to the Driver and can cause out-of-memory errors; and believing that caching eliminates shuffles, when it only avoids recomputation and does not remove the shuffle a wide operation already performed.
s1_definition.analogy: These are the predictable mistakes a clerk at the National Bank of India makes with his desk. Keeping every scrap of paper so the desk overflows and he loses the important ones. Saying "keep this handy" and assuming it is already done when it only happens the first time he actually needs it. Keeping a figure he will use once. Never clearing old summaries during a long shift until the desk is buried. Confusing "keep a copy on your desk" with "bring every original file to my office," which crushes the office. And believing that keeping a sorted pile saves him from the sorting he already did — it does not undo the sort, it just saves re-sorting next time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Do not cache everything, do not assume cache is eager, do not cache single-use data, do not forget unpersist, do not confuse cache with collect, and do not expect cache to remove a shuffle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Common Spark caching mistakes include caching everything indiscriminately, which causes memory pressure and eviction; assuming cache is eager when it is lazy and does nothing until an action; caching data that is used only once, which wastes memory for no reuse benefit; forgetting to unpersist in long-running applications, which lets caches accumulate until storage is exhausted; confusing cache, which stores partitions distributed on executors, with collect, which pulls all data to the Driver and can cause out-of-memory errors; and believing that caching eliminates shuffles, when it only avoids recomputation and does not remove the shuffle a wide operation already performed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** These are the predictable mistakes a clerk at the National Bank of India makes with his desk. Keeping every scrap of paper so the desk overflows and he loses the important ones. Saying "keep this handy" and assuming it is already done when it only happens the first time he actually needs it. Keeping a figure he will use once. Never clearing old summaries during a long shift until the desk is buried. Confusing "keep a copy on your desk" with "bring every original file to my office," which crushes the office. And believing that keeping a sorted pile saves him from the sorting he already did — it does not undo the sort, it just saves re-sorting next time.

**One line to remember:** Do not cache everything, do not assume cache is eager, do not cache single-use data, do not forget unpersist, do not confuse cache with collect, and do not expect cache to remove a shuffle.

sections.s2_technical:
The first mistake is caching everything. Executor storage is finite, so caching indiscriminately fills it and forces eviction, where useful partitions are pushed out and, under memory-only levels, dropped and recomputed. The result is often a job slower than with no caching, plus heavier garbage collection. The fix is to cache deliberately — only datasets that are expensive to compute and reused more than once.

The second mistake is assuming cache is eager. Cache is lazy; it only marks the dataset and does nothing until an action triggers computation. People sometimes call cache and expect the data to be ready, then are surprised the first subsequent action is slow — it is slow because that action is what actually computes and stores the cache. If you want to force materialization at a known point, you run a cheap action like count after caching. The third mistake, closely related, is caching data used only once: with no second read there is nothing to accelerate, so you pay the storage overhead for no benefit.

The fourth mistake is forgetting unpersist in long-running applications. Caches live until evicted or explicitly released, so in a long pipeline or streaming job, caching in each phase without unpersisting accumulates data until storage is exhausted and eviction and recomputation begin. The fix is to unpersist a cache as soon as its reuse is finished. The fifth mistake is confusing cache with collect. These are completely different: cache stores partitions distributed across the executors and the data stays on the cluster, while collect pulls every partition back to the Driver as a single local collection, which on a large dataset can exhaust the Driver's memory and crash the application. Reaching for collect when you meant to cache, or vice versa, is a serious error.

The sixth mistake is believing cache eliminates shuffles. A shuffle happens when a wide operation like groupByKey or join redistributes data across the network, and caching the result of that operation does not undo the shuffle that already occurred — it only avoids recomputing the whole lineage, including that shuffle, on subsequent actions. So caching a post-shuffle dataset means later actions skip re-shuffling, but the first computation still paid the shuffle cost, and caching never removes a shuffle from a single computation. A senior nuance tying these together is that each mistake comes from misunderstanding what caching is: a lazy, distributed, best-effort reuse optimization that preserves lineage, not an eager, durable, or shuffle-removing operation, and not a way to pull data to the Driver. In the bank, the mistakes I most often corrected in code reviews were engineers caching single-use datasets, forgetting unpersist in long jobs, and expecting the first post-cache action to be instant.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An engineer caches every dataset and the job slows down from eviction. This is exactly the cache-everything mistake.

Problem 2 — An engineer assumes cache ran and is surprised the first action is slow. This is exactly the eager-assumption mistake.

Problem 3 — An engineer uses collect expecting caching behavior and crashes the Driver. This is exactly the cache-versus-collect confusion.

The mini-project models a lint-style checker in Java. A `CachingLinter` inspects a planned operation's attributes — cached, reuse count, is-single-use, unpersisted, uses-collect, expects-no-shuffle — and reports each mistake with guidance. The demo runs several realistic banking operations on Rajesh's and Priya's datasets and prints the detected mistakes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: five planned operations, each exhibiting different caching behavior, passed through the linter.

Step 1: The daily extract is cached but reused only once and the engineer assumed cache was eager. The linter flags two mistakes — caching single-use data wastes memory, and cache is lazy so the first action, not the cache call, computes and stores the data.

Step 2: The cleaned transactions are cached and genuinely reused five times, which is good, but it runs in a long job and is never unpersisted. The linter flags one mistake — in a long job, caches accumulate until storage is exhausted, so it must be unpersisted when its reuse ends.

Step 3: The big report uses collect. The linter raises a severe issue because collect pulls all data to the Driver and risks an out-of-memory crash, and this is not caching at all — cache keeps data distributed on the executors.

Step 4: The account totals are cached and reused three times, which is fine, but the engineer expects caching to have removed the groupBy shuffle. The linter flags one mistake — caching does not undo the shuffle that already happened, it only avoids recomputing it on later actions.

Step 5: The machine-learning features are cached, reused twenty times, and unpersisted at the end of the long job. The linter reports no mistakes, confirming correct, deliberate caching.

Step 6: The journey walks through each common mistake and the one correct case, making concrete that caching is a lazy, distributed, best-effort reuse optimization that preserves lineage — not eager, not durable, not a way to pull data to the Driver, and not a shuffle remover.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] 'daily_extract': cached but reused 1x → caching single-use data wastes memory
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] 'daily_extract': cache() is LAZY — first action computes+stores; call count() to materialize if you need it ready
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] 'cleaned_txns': long job without unpersist() → caches accumulate until storage is exhausted
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [SEVERE] 'big_report': collect() pulls ALL data to the Driver (OOM risk) — this is NOT caching; cache() keeps data on executors
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] 'account_totals': cache does NOT remove the shuffle already done; it only avoids recomputing it on LATER actions
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] 'ml_features': caching usage looks correct
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The common caching mistakes all come from misunderstanding what caching actually is, so I group them around that. The first is caching everything: executor storage is finite, so indiscriminate caching fills it and forces eviction, which under memory-only levels means dropping and recomputing partitions, often making the job slower than no caching at all plus heavier garbage collection; the fix is to cache deliberately, only expensive datasets reused more than once. The second is assuming cache is eager, when it is lazy — it only marks the dataset and does nothing until an action, so the first subsequent action is the one that computes and stores it, and if I want to force materialization I run a cheap count. The third, closely related, is caching data used only once, which has no second read to accelerate and just wastes memory.

The fourth is forgetting unpersist in long-running applications, where caches live until evicted or explicitly released, so caching each phase without releasing the previous ones accumulates data until storage is exhausted; the fix is unpersisting a cache as soon as its reuse ends. The fifth is confusing cache with collect, which are completely different — cache stores partitions distributed across the executors with the data staying on the cluster, while collect pulls every partition back to the Driver as one local collection and can exhaust the Driver's memory and crash the application, so using collect when you meant cache is a serious error. The sixth is believing cache eliminates shuffles, when a shuffle from a wide operation like groupByKey or join already happened, and caching the result only avoids recomputing that lineage, including the shuffle, on later actions — the first computation still paid the shuffle, and caching never removes a shuffle from a single computation.

In my project at the National Bank of India these were exactly the issues I most often corrected in code reviews: engineers caching single-use extracts, forgetting unpersist in our long nightly pipelines, and expecting the first post-cache action to be instant. The mental model I reinforce is that caching is a lazy, distributed, best-effort reuse optimization that preserves lineage — not eager, not durable, not a way to pull data to the Driver, and not a shuffle remover. Keeping that definition straight prevents every one of these mistakes.
